name: Interview market making, set 1
description: Market-making questions of the kind interviewers ask: fair values, Fermi estimates, intervals, quote moves, informed flow, limits, hedges and spreads. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: The interviewer deals two cards from a shuffled full deck. An ace counts 1, a number card its number, and a jack, queen or king 10. "Make me a market on the total."
items.question: What is the fair value of the total? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what one card is worth on average, then double it.

byKey.ranks: You counted jack, queen and king as 11, 12 and 13. Here they count 10 each.
byKey.no-courts: You averaged 1 to 10 only. The deck holds four cards worth 10 in each suit, not one.

explain.text: One card averages (1 + 2 + ⋯ + 9 + 4 × 10)/13 = 85/13 ≈ 6.54. Dealing without replacement does not change each card's average. So the total averages 2 × 85/13 = 170/13 ≈ 13.08.

items.prose: A contract pays the larger of two rolls of a fair four-sided die, faces 1 to 4. You quote a market 0.5 wide, centred on fair value.
items.question: What is your bid?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the fair value first, then step half the width down.

byKey.fair: That is the fair value. The bid sits half the width, 0.25, below it.
byKey.offer: That is your offer. The bid is the lower price, 0.25 below fair value.
byKey.one-die: You centred on one die's average, 2.5. The larger of two rolls is worth more.

explain.text: The larger face is m in 2m − 1 of the 16 rolls: 1, 3, 5 and 7 of them. So fair value is (1 + 6 + 15 + 28)/16 = 3.125. Half the width below gives a bid of 3.125 − 0.25 = 2.875.

items.prose: The interviewer asks: how many £1 coins, stacked flat, make a tower as tall as a 20-storey building? Take a storey as about 3 m.
items.question: Which is the best answer to one significant figure?

options.why: You took a coin as about 3 cm thick. It is nearer 3 mm, so the tower needs ten times more.
You stacked the coins by their width, about 2.3 cm. Flat coins stack by their thickness, about 3 mm.
You took a storey as 1 m. At 3 m a storey the building is 60 m tall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the height in millimetres, then divide by a coin's thickness.

explain.text: Twenty storeys at 3 m make about 60 m, or 60,000 mm. A £1 coin is about 3 mm thick, so the tower holds about 20,000 coins. At the true 2.8 mm the count is about 21,400, still 20,000 to one figure.

items.prose: You estimate a café's takings as 400 cups a day at £2.50 a cup: £1,000 a day. Each input could be up to 30% too high or too low.
items.question: Which range must hold the true takings?

options.why: You added the two 30% errors to make 60%. Errors in a product multiply: 0.7 × 0.7 and 1.3 × 1.3.
You allowed for one input's error only. Both can be off in the same direction.
You multiplied the two errors, 0.3 × 0.3 = 9%. Multiply the factors instead: 0.7 × 0.7 and 1.3 × 1.3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the worst-case factors of the two inputs.

explain.text: The product scales by the product of the two factors. At worst both are 0.7, giving 0.49, or both are 1.3, giving 1.69. So the takings lie between £490 and £1,690, a range lopsided upwards.

items.prose: Five fair dice are rolled. The interviewer wants a range for the total that holds at least 90% of the time. The total has mean 17.5 and sd about 3.8.
items.question: Which is the narrowest of these ranges that holds at least 90% of the time?

options.why: It holds 6,862 of the 7,776 rolls, about 88%: just short of 90%.
That is about one sd each side, which holds only about 70%.
It always holds, but it is far wider than 90% needs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go about 1.645 sd each side of the mean, then check the edges.

explain.text: A normal range is 17.5 ± 1.645 × 3.82, about 11.2 to 23.8. Counting the 7,776 rolls, 12 to 23 holds 88.2% and 11 to 24 holds 93.5%. So 11 to 24 is the narrowest of these that passes.

items.prose: You quote 48 at 52, centred on 50. After each trade you move your centre 0.2 of the way to the trade price, keeping the width at 4. A customer buys at your offer, then buys again at your new offer.
items.question: Where is your centre after the two trades?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The offer sits 2 above the centre, so find 0.2 of that gap.

byKey.one-trade: You moved the centre for the first buy only. The second buy moves it another 0.4.
byKey.full-move: You moved the centre all the way to each trade price. The rule moves it only 0.2 of the way.
byKey.wrong-way: You moved the centre down. A buyer at your offer is a reason to move it up.

explain.text: The offer sits 2 above the centre, so each buy moves the centre 0.2 × 2 = 0.4. After the first buy the quote is 48.4 at 52.4, centred on 50.4. The second buy moves the centre to 50.8.

items.prose: A contract settles at 0 or 10 with equal chance, so you quote 4 at 6. One customer in five knows the outcome: they buy when it is 10 and sell when it is 0. The rest buy or sell at random.
items.question: On average, how much do you lose per trade to the informed customers?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the loss on one informed trade, then weight it.

byKey.unweighted: That is the loss on one informed trade. Only one trade in five is informed.
byKey.from-fair: You measured from fair value, 5. The informed customer trades at your price, 6 or 4.
byKey.net: Zero is your net, after the random customers pay the half-width. The question asks for the informed cost alone.

explain.text: An informed customer buys at 6 something worth 10, or sells at 4 something worth 0, so you lose 4. They are one trade in five, so the cost is 0.2 × 4 = 0.8 a trade. The random four in five pay the half-width 1, earning that 0.8 back.

items.prose: You are long 8 lots, and your desk allows at most 10 either way. A customer wants to buy 5 lots from you at your offer.
items.question: What can you do?

options.text: Sell all 5: you end long 3, further inside the limit.
Sell only 2, the room left under the limit.
options.why: Selling makes you less long. The 2 lots of room matter only when you buy.
The customer buys, so you sell. Your position falls to 3, not up to 13.

options.text: Sell 5, then buy 5 elsewhere to stay long 8.
options.why: Buying back undoes the trade that cuts your risk. Long 3 is safer than long 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out which way the trade moves your position.

explain.text: When a customer buys from you, you sell, so your position falls by 5. Long 8 becomes long 3, well inside 10 either way. The limit binds only on trades that push you further long.

items.prose: You are short 40 lots of a contract. Each lot moves 0.45 for every 1 that a liquid hedge moves, in the same direction.
items.question: How many units of the hedge do you buy? A negative number means you sell.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how much the short loses when the hedge rises by 1.

byKey.divided: You divided 40 by 0.45. Each lot is worth 0.45 of a hedge unit, so multiply.
byKey.one-for-one: You hedged one for one. Each lot moves only 0.45 per unit of the hedge.
byKey.sold: Selling adds to the risk of a short. You need a hedge that gains when the contract rises.

explain.text: Short 40 lots lose 40 × 0.45 = 18 for every 1 the hedge rises. Buying 18 units of the hedge gains 18 on the same move. So you buy 18, and the two moves cancel.

items.prose: You quote your centre plus or minus h. Three trades in ten come from someone who knows the value is 4 above or below your centre. They always trade the right way. The other trades are random and pay you h each.
items.question: What full width, bid to offer, makes your average P&L per trade zero?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Balance what random trades pay against what informed trades take.

byKey.half-width: That is the half-width h. The full width runs from bid to offer, 2h.
byKey.net-of-spread: You took your loss to the informed as 4 whatever the width. They gain only 4 − h, since they pay your half-width too.
byKey.double-move: You set the width to the whole move each way. The random trades cover most of the cost.

explain.text: Random trades earn h each, and informed trades cost 4 − h. Break-even needs 0.7h = 0.3(4 − h), so h = 0.3 × 4 = 1.2. The full width is 2 × 1.2 = 2.4.
